txt: A shadow of worry passes over the woman's face. "Oh, my dear Morell. You've been an old man for too long. Kids love to torment insects, almost as much as they love to torment old folks..."
Her eyes light up. "What wonderful news!"
Her eyes light up. "Whatever do you mean?"
Her face flushes with excitement, but she instantly recomposes herself. "I wouldn't be of much use to you, sweetie."
Her grey eyes widen. "Oh my. How would I even begin to tell you? Revachol is the most beautiful city in the world. We're fortunate to be here, you and I."
Like that, she drives off. The gas engine putters quietly, as she gets to the doors -- then pushes them open. Outside the cold coastal wind blows.
She chuckles to herself. "Not at all. Why else would it hide itself so carefully?"
She chuckles. "I'm glad you think so, but I still don't know where you can get cigarettes."
She frowns, looking you over. "Surely things can't be *that* bad?"
She frowns. "Oh dear. Normally I would be happy to talk cryptids all day, but I'm just so frazzled right now, I couldn't tell a tadpole from a fingerling."
She grins. "Can't say no to that. Well... the biggest cryptid is the Giant of Koko Nur."

She grins. "Can't say no to that. Well... the smallest cryptid is the *Cryobacter katlensis*, a unicellular bacterium. It was discovered in one of the northern-most points of Katla on the Boreal Plateau -- by renowned geologist Catelyn Mijanou some 70 years ago."
She grins. "Can't say no to that."
She grins. "I'm glad you liked them, but I'm not really one to tell you about *all* of them. You should ask my husband if you get the chance. He's the real expert."
She laughs. "I doubt it. It's not like teenagers need much encouragement in *that* regard."
She looks at him with tender concern. "Darling, I told you to take it easy. You're getting sick. Maybe it's time to go home?"
She looks at the lieutenant, genially. "...though Seolites do have some distinguishing characteristics, different *advantages*, if you will."
She looks at you, her voice grave suddenly. "It still took the Gnome of Geroma an entire *day* to die."
She looks embarrassed. "Cigarettes are a luxury, sweetie. Besides, I have to mind my health."

She nods gravely. "They tried to communicate with it, and had no other means but sound. So they started sending out sound waves at frequencies they thought might match the Ma Ma Daqua's. And what happens when a sound wave meets another sound wave of the same frequency, dear?"
She nods, but still looks worried.
She nods. "I understand your scepticism, but that's what happens with things that are rare and stand out -- their disappearance is most memorable, and they are least likely to be found again."
She shakes her head slowly.
She sighs. "I know it's not easy, sweetie. But keep thinking about it."
She sighs. "I'm sure it lends you a roguish charm, sweetie."
She sighs. "I've wasted enough of your time with this drama. I really must go before I start crying and waste *more* of it."
She sighs. "I've wasted enough of your time with this drama. I really must stop talking about it, lest I start crying and waste *more* of your time."
She smiles gently. "What about what?"
She smiles, obviously pleased. "I support your decision, officer."
She smiles. "Well, the *biggest* cryptid is -- of course -- the horrible Giant of Koko Nur."
She smiles. "Well, the cryptid on your pen is the kind green ape. Half war story, half undiscovered species in the genus homo."
She smiles. "Well, the most dangerous cryptid is thought to have been the Gnome of Geroma."

She smiles. "Well, the smallest cryptid is the *Cryobacter katlensis*, a unicellular bacterium. It was discovered in one of the northern-most points of Katla on the Boreal Plateau -- by renowned geologist Catelyn Mijanou some 70 years ago."
She turns back to the cafeteria manager. "And there's no public phones nearby?"
She turns to Morell. "Right, honey?"
The old woman's face lights up. "It just means the Insulindian phasmid is even more clever than we thought!"
The woman nods, thoughtfully, while her hands smooth over the plaid covering her knees.
The woman's face flushes with embarrassment. "I'm sorry, sweetie. I'm afraid I'm not very good at this sort of thing."

"'You tryna' tell us you saw the Insulindian phasmid out there in those reeds? Get outta here!'" She smiles. "They'd just give me a cider and ruffle my hair and tell me to stop dreaming -- but I saw it."
"*Cryobacter katlensis*," she answers immediately.
"... where other phasmids imitate sticks or leaves, this one's a living *reed*. It disguises itself among the reeds here on the Insulindian coast."
"...everything has a price, sweetie."
"...they were performed so recklessly that when they happened upon the right frequency... well, they wiped out most of the population."
"A couple of campers found it when it was already dying. They heard an odd wailing in the woods and followed the sound. They were scared and wrapped it in tarpaulin to suffocate it."

"A defeat, I'm afraid. The people of this archipelago tried to build something new, something *different*. The rest of the world didn't like it, so they came and ended it. This was forty two years ago."
"A mirage... or a psychogenous luminance." She does not elaborate the nature of this luminance further.
"A seaside hostel called the Whirling-in-Rags, to be precise. And the Whirling itself is in Revachol."
"A true believer," she looks out the window. "Sometimes I still see it, too. The real memory of it. How it was there... Not the memory *of* the memory. But it's so hard to tell the two apart..."
"Absolutely, sweetie," she smiles, glad you agree. "Cryptozoologists have been tracing it ever since, but Uamrao is vast, mysterious, and holds many secrets."
"Actually, this machine is broken." She taps on the greasy glass of the pinball machine.
"Actually..." She raises her finger. "We are *not*. You could say that about almost any other nation, but not Revachol. Try *one* more time, officer -- what mode of government?"
"After Mijanou treated herself with the bacteria, she stopped ageing, but also became increasingly eccentric and irascible, so that even her oldest friends were forced to pull away..."

"After that, the corpuscle appears to have migrated elsewhere. There have been recordings of anomalies similar to those spotted in Ea -- but they've been few and far between. It's impossible to confirm the presence of any stable Col Do Ma Ma Daqua population anywhere."
"Ah, I'm getting ahead of myself. I was five and a half. In Betancourt, in the suburbs. My grandmother had a summer home there."
"Ah, yes -- probably 'Roll With Me' by The Fletchers. People often quote the Fletchers at me." She settles down. "Morell says it's my theme song."
"Alas, no. And the first scientist who got his hands on the creature's corpse put it in a jar of formaldehyde, thinking that would detoxify the Gnome's venom."
"Alas, the first scientist who got his hands on the creature's corpse put it in a jar of formaldehyde, thinking that would detoxify the Gnome's venom."
"Alone in the blasted desert heat the doctor wandered eastward, where man hasn't stepped foot in over a thousand years -- since the fall of Perikarnassis."

"Although the 'low' part is a little ironic -- the Col Do Ma Ma Daqua makes, or, rather, *is* such a high-pitched sound that other animals, including humans, can't *hear* it. It could be everywhere, all of the time -- and we wouldn't know."
"An old woman in a wheelchair just doesn't look good holding a cigarette. Though I'm sure it lends *you* a roguish charm, sweetie."
"And even if he weren't there, I don't think you'd have much use for *me*." She looks down.
"And have you found anyone to be sweet *to*?" She smiles conspiratorially.
"And if you see him, let him know Lena is waiting for him here at the Whirling. He gets so tangled up in his work that he may not know the water lock's been repaired. And it's *cold* out there..."
"And there's no public phones nearby?"
"And you, detective." She turns to you with a sad smile. "You've been great company to an old lady and her stubborn husband. Thank you, truly."
"Are you sure it was him? Oh, thank heavens! Silly me." She smiles, though there's still concern in her features.
"Aw, thank you, dear. I confess -- I am glad to see it again. Very honourable of you, officer."
"Aw, thank you, dear. I confess -- I am glad to see it again."
"Be friendly, dear," the woman says. "The detective really likes these critters, we've talked about them in great *detail*."
"But -- maybe a *fresh set of eyes* is what the world needs? And -- while I'm no doctor -- such bouts of amnesia are often temporary. So I wouldn't worry *too* much."
"But I am so relieved to hear that he's okay. Thank you for putting an old woman's heart at ease, if even a little."
"But darling, I didn't even get the *size* of it right."
"But if the dream comes to naught, what good is it? No, the thing is..." She looks down at her legs...
"But it *is*. We've spent years searching for the phasmid, hunting it together. Without it, what are we? Just another pathetic old couple..."
"But just one. I doubt your partner would appreciate it if I were to distract you from your duties for much longer!"
"But not you. You're volunteering. So thank you, sweetie."

"But now we're both getting old, and he's still working himself sick out in those reeds, looking for it..." She shakes her head, still unable to meet your eyes. "But what if I was just *wrong*? I think I was..."
"But thank you, sweetie. You did make me forget about my worries for a while." She smiles up at you, but concern is creeping back into her expression.
"But they should have returned by now. They were just going down the coast, across the water lock, to set a few traps. He said they'd be back on Monday..." She sighs. "What could be keeping them?"
"But we should stop for today, sweetie. You look like you need a break. Besides, I'm not the best person to explain the *big* things to anyone..."
"But, dear, you're not for me." She looks off into the distance. "I'm too old, and too married besides."

"Cross the plaza and follow the road along the coast. Down by the water, there will be a shack nestled against an old stone façade. That's the pawnshop. An old friend of my husband's goes there often. He says the owner is quite helpful."
"Did one of these "tiny apes" have a pale green face?" An old woman appears out of the blackness.
"Different -- how?" The half-moons of her glasses reflect you as she looks up at you.
"Do you ever wonder if some lovely story from your childhood is just that... a story? Or a dream?"
"Don't beat yourself up over it too much, dear. People do strange things when the old fight-or-flight kicks in. I'm just glad you weren't injured."
"Either way, I should go. Poor Morell is running a fever and I need to get him home to Jamrock. Before we overstay our welcome with Gary."

"Every now and then, the bird would dive down to feed on an animal carcass somewhere on the horizon. But by the time Uwe got there, the teratorn had taken off already -- and the carcass was picked clean. This happened many times."
"Everyone thought the bacteria had driven her mad. But she really was a brilliant woman -- maybe the Cryobacter katlensis allowed her to see something no one else could..."
"Everything has a price, sweetie."
"Exactly... And these tests were performed so recklessly that when they happened upon the right frequency... well, they wiped out most of the population."

"For years it was a story I told at parties, when I wanted to impress *boys*, that sort of thing." She brushes her hair back. "Of course, most people just took it as a strange, amusing anecdote. So did I, honestly. But then I met Morell..."
"From where I was standing, it looked like you were about to pull out two guns, but drew two... akhem... birdies instead. Well, I'm glad you're weren't injured."

"Gary didn't mean to interfere with your investigation, officers, he's just... thick headed and poor as dirt. But he's always helped us, given us a place to stay. And he's followed Morell into god knows what jungles..."
"Gary's as loyal as they come. I'd trust him with my husband's life any day."
"Gary, what's going on?"
"Good bye." She smiles and they leave -- two old cryptozoologists and one gas-powered wheelchair.
"Good, dear, you got the decade right! It's the spring of '51."
"Goodness! How is he? Did he say why he hasn't returned yet?" The old woman clasps her hands together over her blanket.
"Goodness, no! Well, we did get separated once before, during that *monsoon* in South Safre. But we were younger then, and Morell always takes the appropriate precautions..."
"Granted, kindness may not be an evolutionary advantage..."
"He should be back by now."
"He was lost, without any navigation equipment and desperately low on water. After a day or two he noticed a bird high in the noon sky. A great black bird, it seemed gargantuan."
"He's a scaredy cat." The woman looks at Gary, her eyes motherly.
"He's just on edge because of the lynching. Don't judge him too harshly. Anyway, I'm glad you weren't injured."
"He's right, dear Morell. Come now, we've waited so long, what's one more season?"
"He's so proud of it. He always tells everyone..."
"Hello again, sweetie. I see you've met up with your colleague." She looks at the lieutenant.
"Hello again, sweetie." Her grey eyes shine above the rims of her glasses.
"Hello, dear. It's good to see a familiar face." The elderly woman smiles up at you hopefully.
"Hello, sweetie. How are you?" She sounds tired.
"Hello, sweetie." The elderly woman turns to you with a smile.
"Hello, sweetie."
"Hence its name: The *Insulindian phasmid* -- perhaps you'll end up co-discovering it with us, officer?" She looks you in the eye and nods thoughtfully.
"Here, I want to give you a small token of my gratitude." She hands you a thin ribbon held together by a silver bird skull. "It's a tie, Mesque in origin. The pin is an antique... quite special."

"Hmm... I'm not sure I agree with that, sweetie. At any rate, some argue that the kind green ape should also be thought of as human, especially because it has shown itself to be so *humane*. I don't dare form an opinion one way or the other without more information, though."

"Hmm..." She thinks. "Some argue that the kind green ape should also be thought of as human, especially because it has shown itself to be so *humane*. I don't dare form an opinion one way or the other without more information, though."
"Hmmm. Well, his expression is slightly grumpy, but his eyes are always bright and curious, like a small boy's. And his palms are quite coarse from all the field work, but he's quite gentle..."
"How would I even begin to tell you?" Her grey eyes widen. "Revachol is the most beautiful city in the world. We're fortunate to be here, you and I."
"I absolutely understand, sweetie. It's for the best, believe me. And thank you for everything you've done for us, truly." She nods with a sad little smile.
"I can tell that this is taxing for you, so I'll just ask *one* more question. What regime are we living under? What mode of government?"

"I didn't know this can happen, so I reached my arm and touched the thing. It felt just like a stalk of reed, but it moved. Swaying, towering above me..." She looks at you. "After a while -- 20 seconds? a minute, maybe? -- it left. Went into the reeds."
"I didn't mean to imply that Seolites are in any way inferior to us. In some ways, they are superior -- every species has its advantages and disadvantages."
"I don't know what got into him, officer... Thank you for letting him off easy. He won't forget it; we'll make sure he won't."
"I doubt it, sweetie. The traps aren't big enough for humans to get caught in them. They're for the insect. Anyway..." She looks around.

"I haven't seen very many other cities personally, but everyone says so. Revachol is a rare jewel. This city used to rule the world... Though it has seen better days." There's a pause as she studies your expression. You must look quite lost.
"I hope I've been useful."
"I hope not, although the work you are doing for all of us *is* quite dangerous." Her eyes glimmer with admiration as she looks up at you.
"I hope so! He's going to catch a cold, staying out there for so long..."
"I hope you were able to pawn that old trinket!" She smiles up at you earnestly.
"I knew what I was getting into when I married a *cryptozoologist*, of course. It's just... Waiting for him to come back from field work is always nerve-racking..."

"I looked up and one of the reeds moved. Not like a plant, but like a living thing. It stood up and looked at me. Its body unfolded, like some antique toy..." She shakes her head. "I'd never seen anything like it. The reeds turned into a creature."
"I ran back home to my grandmother and asked her if *reeds* could *walk* and told her they were looking at me." She chuckles. "Of course, she just laughed at me, but I knew what I'd seen..."
"I really would like to help out, but I don't want to slow you down. If it weren't for all the stairs and potholes in Martinaise, I'd join you for sure!" She looks out the window wistfully.
"I see you are still grieving. Well, I won't pry." She smiles gently -- paying no heed to the inexplicable winking.
"I suppose I have something of a *personal* connection to the Insulindian phasmid... All scientists have their little hobby-horses."
"I suppose all of us do at one time or another. I don't know what I'd do without Morell..."
"I suppose you could use a break, and I could use a distraction..."
"I thought we'd agreed on just one cryptid, sweetie."
"I tried, but I was only a child. There was mud and high water, I couldn't see it anymore. I was just standing there, knee deep in mud, looking around me..."
"I understand. Best of luck with your work as well." She smiles up at you, doing her best not to look disappointed.
"I was a paraplegic before we met. He didn't know before I arrived... on our first date. If I weren't the Queen of the Cryptozoologists... If I didn't tell him that story..."
"I was a paraplegic before we met. He didn't know before I came in, on our first date. If I weren't the Queen of the Cryptozoologists... If I didn't tell him that story..."
"I was a training and development manager at a rapidly expanding mail-order shoe company."
"I was also hoping she'd heard from Morell..." She looks down.
"I was lucky. This was almost twenty years ago, and I was compensated exceptionally well. One can only dream of such pay-offs nowadays." She runs her hands over the chrome wheels of her chair.

"I'm Lena. My husband Morell and I are staying with our friend Gary just down the street, but I come here for tea when they're away." Her eyes glitter over the rims of her glasses as she looks up, smiling.
"I'm glad to hear you say it! Smoking can do some real damage to your respiratory system. But I think you already knew that."
"I'm glad you did, dear." She seems genuinely glad.
"I'm not sure of anything." She looks out the window. "Sometimes I still see it, you know. The real memory. Not the memory of the memory, but it's so hard to tell the two apart..."
"I'm sorry if I was being overly familiar! I know we've only just met."
"I'm sorry, dear -- you've had to drudge through them so many times. Such is field work -- a young person's game as they say."
"I'm sorry, dear. It was me -- I made him go home. He gets *so* stubborn about these things -- luckily his cough kept him from arguing with me."
"I'm very grateful to you, sweetie. But -- now that I think about it -- you should talk to Morell about cryptids. He could tell you so much more!"
"I'm worried."
"I'm... in doubt, sweetie. That's all. Everyone is, now and then."
"I'm... not. It's not that..." She doesn't know how to end the sentence.
"If I hadn't led him down this path he could have a steady job lecturing at a university."
"In everyday speech, *human* isn't really a scientific category. For all legal and ethical purposes, your partner is a person just like you, so you might as well *think* of him as being human, too."
"Indeed there is! It's our closest relative among the cryptids. Same taxonomic family, different genus."

"Instead, all the venom leaked out of the creature's teeth and into the surrounding liquid, dissolving the creature itself. A poetic end, perhaps, but a real loss for science..." she says, mostly to herself.
"It *was* reportedly a small creature -- with webbed fingers and a protruding forehead. An ungainly little thing. Quite scary to look at."
"It could be," she says calmly. "As I said, it could be *everywhere*, and we wouldn't know any better. It could be ringing all the days of our lives -- *and* nights."
"It did, yes -- like reeds in a gust of wind."
"It does still look like that in some parts of the city, doesn't it..."
"It doesn't look like it is, sweetie. Are you okay?" An old woman appears out of the blackness.
"It doesn't look so, sweetie. Are you okay?" An old woman appears out of the blackness.
"It happened on a botanical expedition into the vast and unexplored Uamrao canyon in southeast Iilmaraa. Dr. Plattenkalk got separated from his group during a sandstorm..."
"It has something to do with everything. I really don't know how to explain it better..."
"It is quite disappointing, yes. A lot of people would like some form of representation. There's *talk*, but... for now, the RCM is all we've got."
"It means I can't use my legs. I was in an accident some years back, injured *in the line of duty* as they say."
"It seems to me that you lucked out with your partner. He has the look of an upstanding officer of the law, someone you can lean on -- and, sweetie, you *are* looking unsteady."
"It was seen in South Safre during the war, visiting bunkers during the night and healing wounded soldiers with its saliva."
"It's a joke, sweetie. I didn't actually think you saw the Kind Green Ape of South Safre in a hostel in Martinaise. That would be ridiculous. Are you okay?"

"It's easy. You bring a valuable item to a 'pawnbroker' who then gives you money for it. You can get it back later for a slightly larger sum if it hasn't been sold, but you never end up doing that anyway..."
"It's fine, I understand. Thank you anyway." She turns back to you with a weary smile. "I'm glad to see you again, dear."
"It's fine, I understand. Thank you anyway." She turns back to you with a weary smile. "Now, then."
"It's for the best, dear. Lay that story to rest."
"It's hard to say how big things are when you're quite *small* yourself. To me, it seemed to be taller than I was then... but that's probably not the case."
"It's not a hobby, dear. It's a *sub-field* of zoology, one specializing in animal species that are so exceedingly rare that many assume them to be *extinct* or even *fictitious*..."
"It's not easy to assert your right to a decent living wage when you don't have a strong union behind you... Maybe you should talk to Evrart, the Union leader?"
"It's not easy..." She sighs. "I've wasted enough of your time with this drama. I really must stop talking about it, lest I start crying and waste *more* of your time."
"It's not made-up, officer, I can *assure* you."
"It's not. Don't worry. If it were predatory we would have found it by the damage it inflicts."
"It's okay, dear. *Most* hypotheses turn out to be false."
"It's our closest relative among the cryptids. Same taxonomic family, different genus."
"It's really just a *sub-field* of zoology, one specializing in animal species that are so exceedingly rare that many assume them to be *extinct* or even *fictitious*..."
"It's simply *elusive*, so much so that most *establishment* zoologists doubt it exists at all."

"It's the *Col Do Ma Ma Daqua*," the woman corrects her glasses. "Its name means 'thin whisper of sound'. And that's *precisely* what it is -- self-replicating sound waves, invisible and intangible! The Col Do Ma Ma is very afraid of us, which makes it incredibly difficult to track..."
"It's... a strange feeling." She looks down, biting her lower lip. "I haven't really told this to anyone, but... you *are* a police officer."
"Just a moment, officer..." She smiles up at you nervously. "If you run into my husband again... do tell him I'm worried, and to hurry back."
"Just a moment, officer."
"Just a moment." The old woman turns back to the cafeteria manager.
"Just my luck, the phone line is not working..."
"Just some field work, sweetie. Morell is a highly trained scientist. He and his assistant, Gary, are studying an *extremely rare* species of insect..."

"Like nothing. It's such a high-pitched sound that us humans can't hear it -- nor can other animals. It could be ringing right outside your window -- and you wouldn't even know it! It could be anywhere -- everywhere, even..."
"Likewise, sweetie." She flicks a switch on her chair and the engine turns on with a whir. "Thank you for everything. Truly. Even though it turned out to be a..." The sentence remains unfinished.
"Listen, sweetie. I hate to ask, but if your investigation happens to take you to the other side of the coast, please do keep an eye out for my husband..."
"Love can be cruel, sweetie." Her expression turns serious. "Love can be cruel."
"Many scientists have asked the same question -- some have claimed that it isn't *itself* a sound, but a tiny *corpuscle* that emits sound waves. But there's no evidence to support this theory."
"Maybe. But then why do I not dare tell him?" She sighs. "I've wasted enough of your time with this drama. I really must stop talking about it, lest I start crying and waste *more* of your time."
"Mhm, Mijanou did talk about the end of the world a great deal before her abrupt departure."
"Mhm. They grew quite obsessed with these little birds -- even though they couldn't see them, they could distinguish among individual birds and," she smiles, "even began to *name* some of them."
"Mijanou disappeared shortly after injecting herself with the bacteria she had brought back to study -- no doubt, in hopes of prolonging her *own* life."

"More like *he* followed it. A bird that big has many litres of blood in it and he was dying of thirst. For many days, Dr. Plattenkalk followed the teratorn, until they reached a great canyon wall, where the bird finally landed to rest."
"Morell can explain it all much better. I wish you could hear him describe it. Then you'd understand, I'm sure."
"Morell still isn't feeling well. I convinced him to stay at Gary's to get some rest." She looks down at her hands. "I'm afraid the cold has really gotten to him."
"Morell will eventually. Or we'll talk Gary into going back out, perhaps..."
"Morell's so proud of it. He always tells everyone..."

"Much has changed, but it is still the most beautiful city in the world, a rare jewel set in the sand between the pines. Everyone says so, even foreigners." There's a pause as she studies your expression. You must look quite lost.

"My husband did, but it's a shy creature and only shows itself to humans when it feels that it must invervene to save lives. No scientist has ever been able to track it down. It's so mysterious -- I really can't tell you anything more about it."
"My point is, the Insulindian phasmid *probably* does not exist. And you were right to put your bug-chasing days behind you."
"No locusts... but no phasmid either..."
"No one knows for sure. It is like an *awful* mountain appearing from below the horizon and expanding to cover almost a third of your field of vision."
"No problem." She nods, smiling up at you from behind her glasses.
"No! At least... I don't think I did. But Morell was so eager to believe my story was *evidence* of the phasmid's existence..."
"No, dear, I'm not quite *that* old, although I was injured in the line of duty."
"No, dear. But this is basic physics... Oh, sorry, there I go assuming..." She looks flustered for a moment, her eyes full of mute apology, then she recomposes herself. "At any rate, these tests..."
"No, dear. They cancel each other out. And these tests were performed so recklessly that when they happened upon the right frequency... well, they wiped out most of the population."
"No, sweetie," she shakes her head, "there's more to it than that. Morell was so eager to believe my story was *evidence* of the phasmid's existence..."
"No." Her eyes narrow mysteriously. "It's *the* cryptid."
"No." She says -- insisting now. "You don't have to do that. Enough of this fool's errand, Morell will do it. Or Gary. You have work to do, I've wasted enough of everyone's time."
"None of its victims survived. Grieving relatives never even found their bodies because the Gnome's venom dissolved organic tissue almost entirely."

"Nope. Sadly not. Revachol is what's called a Zone of Control. Under an alliance of foreign powers called the Coalition. We have no government of our own and what democracy we have is..." She thinks. "Market driven."
"Not all of them, as far as I remember. But some of them -- on the inside. Like stalks of marble if that makes sense..."
"Nothing so extravagant, dear, though what young girl doesn't dream of soaring over a crowd?"
"Nothing so glamorous, dear, though when I was young, I dreamt of planting the Revacholian flag on some figurative peak."
"Now, gentlemen, no need to squabble." She turns to you. "I wouldn't be of much use to you anyway, sweetie."
"Now, now." She tilts her head as she looks up at you with maternal solicitude.
"Now, what else, sweetie?"
"Of course -- I've thought about it. But Morell says my report matches with the others. And I'm sure I hadn't heard of the phasmid as a child. Nor had my mother -- or my grandmother."
"Of course not -- I didn't mean to say my situation discredits the field. There have been *some* confirmed discoveries. And a lot of hoaxes too, but still..." She looks to the door.
"Of course, dear! I just wish I could have done more."
"Of course, dear. Good luck with your case!" She gives you a small wave.
"Of course, dear. Is there a particular cryptid that you're interested in learning about?"
"Of course, dear."
"Of course, most phasmid sightings turn out to be *false alarms*, but their description matched the Insulindian phasmid *perfectly*, and they didn't even know what they were looking at!"
"Of course, officers." She smiles politely. "Is there a particular cryptid you two are interested in learning about?"
"Of course, sweetie, I... I really don't know how to explain it better."
"Of course, sweetie, you've helped us so much already. Everyone would understand if you..."
